content: The quality of evidence was categorized as high, moderate, low, or very low, following the definitions outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. GRADE tables were created using the GRADEpro software when applicable. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses are accessible through online annexes (URLs provided) and will be published. Based on these data and reviews, the WHO Steering Committee proposed an initial set of draft recommendations. The WHO Steering Committee, composed of members from the Department of Maternal, Newborn, Child and Adolescent Health and the Department of Nutrition for Health and Development, supervised the guideline review process. Annex 6 provides a list of WHO staff members on the committee. The WHO convened a 17-member Guideline Development Group, consisting of internationally recognized experts in content, methodology, and regional representation. Annex 6 lists the members of this group. These external experts contributed to the development of evidence-informed recommendations and helped finalize the scope and key questions of the guideline in PICO format. This group was established early in the guideline development process, after the Steering Committee defined the general scope and began drafting key questions. Members were selected to ensure a range of technical skills, diverse perspectives, and geographic representation. An external peer-review group was tasked with reviewing the recommendations developed by the Guideline Development Group. Their role was to ensure no significant omissions, contradictions, or inconsistencies with scientific evidence or programmatic feasibility. They also assisted in clarifying the language, particularly regarding implementation and how policymakers and program staff might interpret the recommendations. No additional recommendations were solicited from this group. The WHO Steering Committee compiled the queries raised by the external peer-review group and discussed them with the chairs to resolve any inconsistencies or contradictions. Annex 6 lists the members of the external peer-review group, including their affiliations and countries of origin. All members of the Guideline Development Group, systematic review teams, and the external peer-review group were required to sign and submit declarations of interest and confidentiality forms before participating in meetings. The WHO Steering Committee reviewed these declarations to identify any potential conflicts of interest that might preclude or limit participation. One potential conflict of interest was noted: Professor Linda Adair disclosed that her affiliated institution had received funding from Wyeth in 2012 and from 2012 to 2014. Wyeth was acquired by Nestlé in 2013. Professor Adair did not personally receive any funds for herself or her research. After discussion with the WHO Department of Compliance, Risk Management, and Ethics, it was agreed that Professor Adair could attend the meeting, present data, and contribute to discussions. However, she would not be eligible to vote on recommendations. These details were disclosed to all participants at the start of the meeting, and the approach was agreed upon. No other potential conflicts of interest were declared by members of the Guideline Development Group. The Guideline Development Group used the GRADE method to evaluate the quality of evidence. GRADE tables summarized details about the included studies, such as study outcomes, limitations (risk of bias), potential inconsistencies, indirectness, imprecision, and other factors affecting the quality of evidence. Definitions of the levels of evidence quality using the GRADE method are provided in Annex 6. Evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) was initially rated as high quality, while evidence from observational studies was rated as low quality. These initial ratings could be downgraded based on factors such as study limitations, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and reporting or publication bias. Conversely, non-randomized studies could be upgraded based on factors like dose-response gradients, the directional effect of plausible bias, and the magnitude of effect. For each draft recommendation, the WHO Steering Committee presented a synthesis of evidence, GRADE tables, and draft recommendation language. Decision-making tables were drafted, considering the benefits and risks of interventions from a public health perspective, the values and preferences of mothers and communities, and the feasibility of implementation, particularly in resource-limited settings. The cost of options available to healthcare workers was not formally assessed due to a lack of primary data but was considered in general discussions. Comments were based on personal experiences and extrapolations from general cost considerations. Each member of the Guideline Development Group reviewed the material and independently provided comments and suggested revisions to the proposed guidance and decision-making tables. They were asked to rank the overall quality of evidence using the GRADE method, assess the balance of benefits versus harm, consider the values relevant to making a recommendation, and evaluate the applicability of recommendations to the intended populations. They also assessed the strength of each recommendation based on predefined criteria. Strong recommendations indicated that the desirable effects of adherence outweighed the undesirable effects, making them suitable for adoption as policy in most situations. Conditional recommendations were made when the desirable effects probably outweighed the undesirable effects but were applicable only to specific groups, populations, or settings. Conditional recommendations required substantial debate and stakeholder involvement before adoption as policy. In cases where further research was needed, no recommendation was made. The Guideline Development Group used a consensus-building process to finalize recommendations. If consensus could not be reached, a simple majority vote would determine contested decisions. WHO staff did not express personal opinions on the data, discussions, or decisions regarding recommendation language, strength, or evidence quality. Instead, they articulated the principles and guidelines of the WHO decision-making process. The group reached agreement on all recommendations and best practice statements without requiring a final vote. The guideline will be disseminated through the WHO website, including the Child Health and Nutrition sections, the WHO e-Library of Evidence for Nutrition Actions (eLENA), and social media. Recommendations will be shared with international partners, WHO country and regional offices, health ministries, collaborating centers, other UN agencies, and non-governmental organizations. Assistance will be provided to adapt the guideline to national contexts as needed. WHO publications, including training materials for populations of infants and children, will be revised to reflect the guideline. Countries are expected to adapt the recommendations to their local social, cultural, and economic contexts. Stakeholder discussions will be encouraged to inform decision-making on using and introducing the recommendations into national programs. Frameworks like DECIDE (Developing and Evaluating Communication Strategies to Support Informed Decisions and Practice Based on Evidence) will be shared to assist policymakers. An enabling environment, including relevant national policies and changes in healthcare practitioner behavior, should be created to support evidence-informed practices. Monitoring and evaluation should be integrated into the implementation process to provide lessons for further uptake and implementation. National child health programs should collect and report data on child health, including the prevalence of wasting, stunting, overweight, and obesity, as well as growth patterns among infants and children with a history of low birth weight. Implementation research will inform and assist policy adoption and implementation. The WHO Secretariat will continue to monitor research developments, particularly for questions where the quality of evidence was low or very low, to update the guideline as needed.
